title: Anatomy, Thorax, Brachiocephalic (Innominate) Veins -- Introduction
content: The brachiocephalic veins, also called the "innominate veins," are large venous structures located within the thorax and originate from the union of the subclavian vein with the internal jugular vein. The left and right brachiocephalic veins join to form the superior vena cava (SVC) on the right side of the upper chest. These vessels constitute a vital component of the human circulatory system, facilitating drainage of deoxygenated blood from the head and upper limbs.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Brachiocephalic (Innominate) Veins -- Introduction
content: The role of the brachiocephalic veins in systemic venous return makes them important in the diagnosis and management of vascular obstruction, thrombosis, or complications related to central venous access. Surgical approaches to the mediastinum and aortic arch often require careful consideration of the brachiocephalic veins, as inadvertent injury can result in significant hemorrhage or compromise of venous return. A comprehensive understanding of the anatomy and physiology of these blood vessels allows clinicians to interpret imaging findings, optimize procedural safety, anticipate potential complications, and implement effective management strategies.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Brachiocephalic (Innominate) Veins -- Structure and Function
content: The brachiocephalic veins are formed by the confluence of the subclavian vein and the internal jugular vein on the right and left, respectively. Both the brachiocephalic veins and the SVC are valveless vessels. The left brachiocephalic vein is generally longer than the right due to the anatomic position of the SVC on the right side of the middle mediastinum, which allows the left vein to bypass the aortic arch (see Image . Vascular Structures of the Upper Thorax). The right brachiocephalic vein typically measures 2 to 3 cm, whereas the left measures approximately 6 cm. [1]

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Brachiocephalic (Innominate) Veins -- Structure and Function
content: The right brachiocephalic vein is related to the cartilage of the 1st rib, the sternothyroid (an infrahyoid muscle), the phrenic nerve, cranial nerve X, the parietal pleura, and the brachiocephalic arterial trunk. The left brachiocephalic vein courses inferiorly from the region of the clavicle at an oblique angle, generally passing anterior to the aortic arch. This blood vessel maintains relationships with the medial epiphysis of the clavicle, the sternothyroid and sternohyoid, and retrosternal fat.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Brachiocephalic (Innominate) Veins -- Structure and Function
content: The primary function of the brachiocephalic veins is to carry deoxygenated blood from the systemic circulation back to the right side of the heart and, subsequently, to the pulmonary circuit for oxygenation. [2] Blood from the head drains via the internal jugular veins, whereas blood from the upper extremities drains via the subclavian veins. Additional vessels that empty into the brachiocephalic veins include the left and right inferior thyroid veins, the left and right internal thoracic veins, and the left superior intercostal vein. [3]

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Brachiocephalic (Innominate) Veins -- Structure and Function
content: Each vein consists of multiple layers. The outer layer, or adventitia, is composed of connective tissue. The middle layer, or tunica media, is composed of smooth muscle cells. The inner layer, or tunica intima, consists of endothelial cells.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Brachiocephalic (Innominate) Veins -- Embryology
content: The brachiocephalic veins derive from the cardinal venous system. [4] Three pairs of cardinal veins comprise this system, which begins to drain the embryo's body during the 5th week of development. The right brachiocephalic vein develops from the proximal right anterior cardinal vein, the right common cardinal vein, and the right horn of the sinus venosus. The left anterior cardinal vein gives rise to the left brachiocephalic vein. [5] The layer of embryological derivation is the mesoderm.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Brachiocephalic (Innominate) Veins -- Blood Supply and Lymphatics
content: Lymphatic vessels within the thorax converge to form bronchomediastinal trunks. The trunks on the right side are typically located along the right brachiocephalic vein and the subserosal surface of the mediastinal pleura. The bronchomediastinal trunks on the left side of the body display more variable courses. [6] The thoracic duct, responsible for the majority of the body’s lymphatic drainage, enters the venous system most often at the junction of the left internal jugular vein and left subclavian vein near the origin of the left brachiocephalic vein. [7] Tributaries to the brachiocephalic veins include the right and left internal mammary veins, the pericardiophrenic veins, the right and left superior intercostal veins, and the inferior thyroid vein, which terminates into the left brachiocephalic vein.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Brachiocephalic (Innominate) Veins -- Nerves
content: The right phrenic nerve lies posterior and lateral to the right brachiocephalic vein. The right vagus nerve courses posteriorly in the thorax, forming the posterior vagal trunk. The left phrenic and vagus nerves run near the left brachiocephalic vein, with the left vagus nerve forming the anterior vagal trunk. [8]

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Brachiocephalic (Innominate) Veins -- Muscles
content: The brachiocephalic veins lie adjacent to the muscles of the inferior neck. The confluence of the subclavian and internal jugular veins, forming the brachiocephalic veins, is located at the medial border of the anterior scalene muscle. [9] The anterior scalene lies deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle and inserts on the scalene tubercle of the 1st rib. The subclavian vein passes anterior to the anterior scalene muscle to unite with the internal jugular vein, whereas the subclavian artery and brachial plexus pass posterior to the same muscle.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Brachiocephalic (Innominate) Veins -- Physiologic Variants
content: Physiologic anomalies of the brachiocephalic veins are rare, yet they have been documented in the literature. The most common variant involves anomalous veins traversing the space beneath the aortic arch and above the pulmonary artery, crossing in front of the ligament arteriosum or, if present, a patent ductus arteriosus. Other reported variants include brachiocephalic veins that cross the midline above the aortic arch or behind a patent ductus arteriosus. These variations sometimes coexist with other great vessel anomalies, such as a bilateral SVC or a double aortic arch.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Brachiocephalic (Innominate) Veins -- Physiologic Variants
content: At least 1 documented case of an absent SVC reports a variant course of the right brachiocephalic vein, which continues posteriorly as the azygos vein before crossing to the left side of the spinal column. The left brachiocephalic vein continues directly posteriorly and inferiorly as the accessory hemiazygos vein and joins the azygos vein at the level of the 6th thoracic vertebra on the left side. In this instance, venous drainage of the upper body enters the right atrium entirely via the inferior vena cava. [10]

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Brachiocephalic (Innominate) Veins -- Surgical Considerations
content: The left brachiocephalic vein may hinder a surgical approach to the aortic arch during cardiac procedures performed via median sternotomy. In such cases, documentation indicates that the surgeon can safely divide the left brachiocephalic vein to improve access to the aortic arch. Reconstruction of the vein has not demonstrated a proven benefit. Long-term anticoagulation following division has also not been shown to be necessary. The main concern after division of the left brachiocephalic vein is swelling of the left neck and upper limb, which generally resolves with conservative management as collateral drainage develops via the azygos–hemiazygos system, the internal mammary veins, the lateral thoracic and superficial thoracoabdominal veins, the vertebral venous plexus, and the transverse sinus. [11]

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Brachiocephalic (Innominate) Veins -- Surgical Considerations
content: Another scenario that often necessitates consideration of the brachiocephalic veins is resection of mediastinal tumors. Tumors that invade the SVC, and, therefore, warrant resection and reconstruction of the SVC, have been well documented to require temporary bypass between the brachiocephalic veins and the right atrium using a small-diameter catheter. [12]

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Brachiocephalic (Innominate) Veins -- Clinical Significance
content: The brachiocephalic veins are essential central venous access sites and are frequent locations for placement of central venous catheters (CVCs) or venous chemotherapy ports. Advances in ultrasound-guided technology have made access to these structures both feasible and safe. [13] The possibility of vein stenosis following long-term CVC placement should be considered. Another rare but well-documented risk of CVC placement is the formation of a brachiocephalic vein pseudoaneurysm.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Brachiocephalic (Innominate) Veins -- Other Issues
content: Compression of the brachiocephalic vein may result from mediastinal masses. Although rare, bilateral brachiocephalic vein compression is often clinically indistinguishable from SVC obstruction.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Brachiocephalic (Innominate) Veins -- Other Issues
content: A recent case report described a thymic neuroendocrine tumor presenting as an asymptomatic anterior thoracic mass measuring 8 cm. This tumor can involve various anatomical structures, including the brachiocephalic veins. In this clinical case, the veins were removed. [14] A thymoma, a rare cancer originating from the thymic gland, can involve the left brachiocephalic vein through direct invasion or extension via the thymic veins, forming a tumor thrombus. [15]

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Brachiocephalic (Innominate) Veins -- Other Issues
content: A recent review highlighted that stent placement in the brachiocephalic veins requires constant reevaluation and potential reintervention. The veins are less compliant, making ongoing assessment necessary to optimize long-term patency. [16]

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Brachiocephalic (Innominate) Veins -- Other Issues
content: Traumatic injury may, in rare cases, involve the brachiocephalic vein, particularly in high-speed or penetrating accidents affecting the cervicomediastinal region, often in the presence of fractures of the ribs, clavicle, or sternoclavicular joint. Imaging may reveal a mediastinal or perivascular hematoma. Catheter-directed angiography is recommended to enhance safety and determine the most appropriate procedure. [17] During right-heart catheterization, the distal brachiocephalic vein may be injured, evident on CT with contrast leakage. [18]
